targetQuery: C# string immutability, UTF-16 length surprises ("😀".Length==2), grapheme clusters vs code points, Turkish-I culture bug, Span<char> vs Substring allocation, StringBuilder cost
comparedAgainst: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string — fetched in full. Confirms the immutability claim ('A String object is called immutable (read-only), because its value cannot be modified after it has been created') and, verbatim, the quoted phrase 'creates a new String object for each concatenation operation' used in the naive-concatenation section.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/character-encoding-introduction — fetched in full. Confirms char = 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, surrogate pairs, code point vs scalar value vs grapheme cluster/text element terminology, and the specific claim that 'prior to .NET 5, the StringInfo class had a bug causing some grapheme clusters to be handled incorrectly' — matches the article's citation exactly.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/best-practices-strings — fetched in full. Confirms the Turkish-I problem exactly as described (İ = U+0130, ı = U+0131, tr-TR and az cultures), confirms String.Equals/== default to ordinal, and confirms the explicit recommendation to use StringComparison.Ordinal/OrdinalIgnoreCase 'as your safe default for culture-agnostic string matching' — matches the article's guidance claim.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.span-1 — fetched in full. Confirms the exact two costs quoted for Substring ('Creates a new string to hold the substring' / 'Copies a subset of the characters from the original string to the new string') and the ref-struct/stack-only restrictions (cannot be boxed, stored in a field of a reference type, or used across await) that the article states.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.intern — fetched in full. Confirms 'the memory allocated for interned String objects is not likely to be released until the common language runtime (CLR) terminates' and that interning still requires creating the string first — supports the article's 'lives for the rest of the process' / 'requires building the string first' claims, though this specific sentence (line ~76) has no inline citation of its own (see issues).

www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U10300.pdf and U10330.pdf (Unicode Standard 18.0 code charts) — fetched directly. Old Italic is U+10300–U+1032F; U+10330 is the *first* code point of the separate Gothic block (U+10330–U+1034F): U+10330 = GOTHIC LETTER AHSA, U+10331 = GOTHIC LETTER BAIRKAN. The article's Rune section names these two code points as Old Italic letters — they are not (see issues).
justification:
Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs` against the worktree copy of the article: PASS, blocks=18, executed=9, and reran it — deterministic, byte-for-byte identical output each time, including the concatenation-benchmark byte counts (400,519,976 / 49,248 / 1,601,039,976) and the Span/Substring byte counts (32 B / 0 B), because `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread` measures exact bytes rather than wall time. I independently reproduced the key 'surprising' claims from scratch in throwaway file-based programs on the same machine (.NET 10.0.401): '😀'.Length == 2 (confirmed, and confirmed against Microsoft's own character-encoding-introduction page, which shows the same surrogate-pair behavior for a different emoji); StringBuilder's default capacity of 16 and doubling growth (16→32→64→128→256, confirmed empirically by watching `Capacity` after each `Append`); and the Turkish-I culture switch (en-US 'i'.ToUpper()=='I' vs tr-TR 'i'.ToUpper()=='İ', with OrdinalIgnoreCase unaffected) — all matched the article exactly and matched Microsoft's own worked Turkish-I example (same İ/ı code points, same tr-TR/az culture list) on the best-practices-strings page.

**Escape-sequence check (item 1): PASS.** Dumped the raw bytes of the `three-counts` sample array (`od -c`) directly from the on-disk worktree file. Both `"cafe\u0301"` and `"caf\u00e9"` are literal ASCII text — backslash, 'u', then four hex digits, as separate characters in the byte stream — not raw combining or precomposed Unicode characters. The writer's claimed fix genuinely held; there is no silent-conversion regression in this file.

**Byte-count internal consistency (item 3): consistent with the O(n²) model, but one arithmetic claim is wrong.** Modeling each `+=` allocation as a string object of length L costing roughly 24+2L bytes and summing L=1..N gives N²+25N, which predicts ≈400,500,000 B at N=20,000 and ≈1,601,000,000 B at N=40,000 — both within noise of the article's actual measured 400,519,976 and 1,601,039,976, so the O(n²) shape is real and the two numbers are mutually consistent. However, the article states the ratio between them is '3.998x, to be precise'; the actual ratio (verified with exact integer arithmetic, not floating point) is 1,601,039,976 / 400,519,976 = 3.997403..., which rounds to 3.997x, not 3.998x. This is exactly the kind of exact-digit claim the article's own framing ('to be precise') invites a reader to check, and it is off by one in the third decimal.

**A genuine factual error, independent of the three checklist items: Gothic mislabeled as Old Italic.** The 'Rune type' section (code block id=rune-letters) uses `\U00010330\U00010331` with the comment `// "ok" + two Old Italic letters (outside the BMP)`, and the surrounding prose says 'the Old Italic script (`U+10330` onward), which needs a surrogate pair per letter'. I fetched the actual Unicode Standard 18.0 code charts directly from unicode.org: the Old Italic block is U+10300–U+1032F. U+10330 is the *first* code point of a separate block, Gothic (U+10330–U+1034F): U+10330 is GOTHIC LETTER AHSA and U+10331 is GOTHIC LETTER BAIRKAN. The code still runs and still correctly demonstrates the char-vs-Rune classification point (both code points are genuinely OtherLetter category, confirmed via `Rune.GetUnicodeCategory`), so the *mechanism* the section teaches is undamaged, but the article confidently names the wrong script for its own worked example — on an article whose entire premise is 'these claims are exactly right, and we ran them to prove it.' Per the brief's scoring rule, a single factual error caps the technical score at 7.

**Citation integrity: strong, one placement nit.** Every source I spot-checked (String, character-encoding-introduction, best-practices-strings, Span<T>, String.Intern) was fetched in full and supports the specific clause it is cited for, including exact verbatim quotes. One minor placement issue: the sentence 'an interned string typically lives for the rest of the process, and interning still requires building the string first' (line ~76) is not itself inline-cited, though it is accurate and supported by String.Intern's Performance Considerations remarks, and the intern-pool citation appears earlier in the same paragraph for a related clause.

No other factual, code-behavior, or citation problems found. Depth is genuinely strong: empirically measured allocation costs (not just Big-O assertions), a real predict-then-verify exercise with exact byte arithmetic, three independently-run counting APIs compared side by side, and honest scoping of implementation-detail claims (StringBuilder capacity growth, string object layout) that goes beyond what a typical blog post attempts.

issues.location: Prose above code block id=rune-letters (~line 232: 'such as the Old Italic script (`U+10330` onward)...') and the code block itself (~line 237: `string word = "ok\U00010330\U00010331"; // "ok" + two Old Italic letters (outside the BMP)`), and the surrounding paragraph (~line 256)
issues.problem: U+10330 and U+10331 are not Old Italic letters. Per the Unicode Standard 18.0 code charts (fetched directly from unicode.org), Old Italic occupies U+10300–U+1032F; U+10330 is the first code point of the distinct Gothic block (U+10330–U+1034F). U+10330 = GOTHIC LETTER AHSA, U+10331 = GOTHIC LETTER BAIRKAN. The article misidentifies the script by name in both the prose and the code comment.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either (a) rename every mention of 'Old Italic' in this section to 'Gothic' (the code, output, and pedagogical point about char vs Rune classification are otherwise unaffected — Gothic is also outside the BMP and both code points are still classified OtherLetter), or (b) keep 'Old Italic' and swap the code points to ones actually inside U+10300–U+1032F, e.g. U+10300 (OLD ITALIC LETTER A) and U+10301 (OLD ITALIC LETTER BE). Either way, cite the relevant Unicode block chart (unicode.org/charts/PDF/U10300.pdf for Old Italic or U10330.pdf for Gothic) to make the script identification independently verifiable.
